passages.t: To Philemon and the church in his house
passages.happening: “Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, To Philemon our beloved fellow worker, to Apphia our sister, to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church that meets at your house: Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (verses 1-3).
passages.hearers:
Paul often opens a letter by calling himself an apostle. Here he calls himself ‘a prisoner of Christ Jesus’. He is in chains, but he does not see himself as Rome's prisoner. He belongs to Christ, even in prison. And this is a letter that will ask for something hard, written by a man who has given up a great deal himself.

Philemon is a ‘beloved fellow worker’, a friend who has worked beside Paul for the gospel. Apphia is ‘our sister’ and Archippus ‘our fellow soldier’. We know little more about them. Archippus is also given a message in Colossians (Colossians 4:17), and that, with Onesimus being called ‘one of you’ in the same letter (Colossians 4:9), is why most readers place Philemon in the town of Colossae.

Then comes ‘the church that meets at your house’. There were no church buildings. Believers met in homes, and a house church gathered the household itself: family, slaves, freed slaves and neighbours. So this letter, though it is about a private matter, will be read out in front of the whole church. Philemon will hear Paul's request with everyone listening, perhaps including Onesimus. Paul means it to be that way.
passages.ot:
Paul's ‘grace and peace’ echo the blessing God gave Israel's priests to speak over the people: “may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:25-26).

And the God who gathers his people into one household is the God of the psalms: “God settles the lonely in families” (Psalm 68:6).
passages.asks: Paul writes to a whole church about one relationship, because how believers treat each other is everyone's business. Ask whether there is a relationship in your life that your church family would be troubled to see as it really is. And ask who in your church you think of as a fellow worker, a sister, a brother.

passages.happening:
“I always thank my God, remembering you in my prayers, because I hear about your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints” (verses 4-5).

“I pray that your partnership in the faith may become effective as you fully acknowledge every good thing that is ours in Christ. I take great joy and encouragement in your love, because you, brother, have refreshed the hearts of the saints” (verses 6-7).
passages.hearers:
Paul begins with real praise. Philemon has faith in Jesus and love ‘for all the saints’, all the believers. He has opened his home, and his kindness has ‘refreshed the hearts of the saints’, like cool water on a hot day.

Notice the word ‘partnership’. In Greek it is koinōnia, which means sharing, fellowship, having things in common. Paul prays that Philemon's sharing in the faith will become ‘effective’, that it will show itself in action. He is quietly getting ready for his request.

Notice too the word ‘hearts’. The Greek word means the inner parts, the place of the deepest feelings, much as we use ‘heart’. It will come back twice: Onesimus is Paul's ‘very heart’ (verse 12), and Paul will ask Philemon to ‘refresh my heart’ (verse 20). Philemon has refreshed the hearts of so many. Paul is about to ask him to do it once more, in the hardest place.

‘For all the saints.’ Paul does not yet say that Onesimus is now one of the saints. But that is where the letter is going.
passages.ot:
The psalms delight in the people of God living as one family: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony!” (Psalm 133:1).

And Proverbs knows how much good a kind word can do: “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver” (Proverbs 25:11).
passages.asks: Paul thanks God for a friend whose love refreshed others. Ask whose love has refreshed you, and whether you have thanked them. Ask whether your love reaches ‘all the saints’, or only some of them. And ask whether your faith is becoming effective, showing itself in what you do.

passages.t: An appeal of love for Onesimus, once useless, now useful
passages.happening:
“So although in Christ I am bold enough to order you to do what is proper, I prefer to appeal on the basis of love. For I, Paul, am now aged, and a prisoner of Christ Jesus as well” (verses 8-9).

“I appeal to you for my child Onesimus, whose father I became while I was in chains. Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me” (verses 10-11).
passages.hearers:
Paul says he could give an order. He is an apostle, and Philemon owes him a great deal. But he chooses to ‘appeal’, to ask, and he asks ‘on the basis of love’. He wants Philemon to act freely, not because he was told to.

He also reminds Philemon who is asking: an old man, in chains. That is not a trick. It is the truth, and it is part of why Philemon should listen.

Only now, in verse 10, does Paul name the man the letter is about: ‘my child Onesimus, whose father I became while I was in chains’. While Paul was in prison, Onesimus came to faith in Christ through him. Paul now thinks of him as his own son.

Then comes a joke with a serious point. The name Onesimus means ‘useful’. It was a common name for slaves, the kind of name an owner gave. Paul says he was once ‘useless’ to Philemon but is now ‘useful’ to both of them. In the Greek of the day, the word for ‘useful’ also sounded much like ‘Christ’. Something has happened to Onesimus. He has met Christ, and he has become what his name always said.

What had Onesimus done to make him ‘useless’ to Philemon? The letter does not say.
passages.ot:
God is a father to those who have none: “A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in His holy habitation” (Psalm 68:5).

And Israel's law protected a slave who had escaped: “Do not return a slave to his master if he has taken refuge with you. Let him live among you wherever he chooses, in the town of his pleasing. Do not oppress him” (Deuteronomy 23:15-16).
passages.hard:
What do we actually know about Onesimus, and what have readers inferred?

The letter says that Onesimus belonged to Philemon as a slave (verse 16), that he had been ‘separated’ from him ‘for a while’ (verse 15), that he came to faith through Paul while Paul was in chains (verse 10), and that Paul was sending him back (verse 12). It also says, ‘if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account’ (verse 18). That is all.

The rest is inference, and readers infer different things. Many read the letter, as early interpreters such as John Chrysostom did, to mean that Onesimus ran away, perhaps after stealing something, and that verse 18 points to the loss. Some read him as a slave who went to Paul, a friend of his master, to ask him to plead his case in a quarrel; Roman legal writers knew of such slaves and did not count them as runaways. Others think Philemon had sent him to help Paul. Each view explains some details and strains at others.

The letter does not say that Onesimus ran away, and it does not say that he stole. These notes do not choose. What the letter does say is that, whatever had happened, Onesimus was now Paul's child in the faith, and Paul was putting himself between him and any debt.
passages.asks: Paul could command but chose to appeal in love. Ask where you use pressure or position to get what you want, when you could ask. Ask whether there is someone you have written off as ‘useless’, whom Christ may have changed. And ask whether you are quick to assume the worst about someone's past when you do not know it.

passages.t: No longer as a slave, but as a beloved brother
passages.happening:
“I am sending back to you him who is my very heart. I would have liked to keep him with me, so that on your behalf he could minister to me in my chains for the gospel. But I did not want to do anything without your consent, so that your goodness will not be out of compulsion, but by your own free will” (verses 12-14).

“For perhaps this is why he was separated from you for a while, so that you might have him back for good— no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother. He is especially beloved to me, but even more so to you, both in person and in the Lord” (verses 15-16).
passages.hearers:
Paul is sending Onesimus back, and it costs him. Onesimus is ‘my very heart’. Paul would have liked to keep him, to help him in prison. But he will not do it without Philemon's agreement. He wants Philemon's goodness to be freely given.

Then Paul looks at what happened in a new light. ‘Perhaps’ this is why they were apart for a while: so that Philemon could have Onesimus back ‘for good’, for ever. Notice the ‘perhaps’. Paul does not claim to know God's reasons, and he does not say that whatever had gone wrong was good.

Then comes the heart of the letter. Philemon is to have Onesimus back ‘no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother’. In Roman law, Onesimus was still Philemon's property. Paul says that is no longer the most important thing about him. He is a brother.

And look at the last words: ‘both in person and in the Lord’. ‘In person’ is, word for word, ‘in the flesh’, in everyday life. Paul does not say Onesimus is a brother only at church, while he stays a slave the rest of the week. He is a brother in the house, at the table, at work. A master who heard that and meant it could not keep treating his brother as a thing he owned.
passages.ot:
When brothers who had been parted were reunited in Genesis, they did not meet as master and servant. Jacob came to Esau bowing as a servant, but “Esau, however, ran to him and embraced him, threw his arms around his neck, and kissed him. And they both wept” (Genesis 33:4).

Israel's law told Israelites not to treat a fellow Israelite who had to sell himself as a slave: “Let him stay with you as a hired worker or temporary resident” (Leviticus 25:40). And Job said why no master is above his servant: “Did not He who made me in the womb also make them? Did not the same One form us in the womb?” (Job 31:15).
passages.hard:
Why does Paul send Onesimus back, and why does he not tell Philemon to set him free?

Paul does not say that slavery is wrong, and he does not, in so many words, command Onesimus's freedom. That should not be softened. He was a prisoner with no power over Roman law, writing to a tiny community, and an open call for slaves to be freed could have brought violent suspicion on the church. But he asks for far more than the law required, and he plants something slavery could not hold: a slave who is a brother ‘in person and in the Lord’, a master who owes him a welcome, and both equal in one church. Later Christians drew that out, from Gregory of Nyssa in the 300s, who preached against owning human beings at all, to the evangelical abolitionists of the 1700s and 1800s. The church was slow, and its slowness is part of its history to be confessed, not defended.

The history of this letter is painful. Before the American Civil War, defenders of slavery cited it as proof that the apostle returned a runaway to his master, and used it to support the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 and to defend slavery as biblical. That was a misuse, and it was wrong. Paul sent Onesimus back ‘no longer as a slave’ and ‘as a beloved brother’, with his own name and money on the line for him. Atlantic slavery, built on race and kidnapping, was very different from the Roman kind, and the law of Moses punished kidnapping with death. Abolitionists answered from this very verse, and enslaved Christians often heard the Bible very differently from the way it was preached to them.

Nor is this letter a rule for work today, or a lesson for any party. A worker is not property, and no one should use it to tell anyone to go back to a place where they are mistreated. The Honest Answer ‘Why didn't the Bible just ban slavery?’ goes further.
passages.asks: Paul asks Philemon to see Onesimus as a brother in everyday life, not only at church. Ask whether there is someone you call a brother or sister in Christ but treat as less than that the rest of the week. Ask whether you hold any power over someone that the gospel is asking you to use differently. And ask what it would cost you to receive someone back for good.

passages.t: Receive him as me; charge it to my account
passages.happening:
“So if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me. But if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account. I, Paul, write this with my own hand. I will repay it—not to mention that you owe me your very self” (verses 17-19).

“Yes, brother, let me have some benefit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ. Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I ask. In the meantime, prepare a guest room for me, because I hope that through your prayers I will be restored to you” (verses 20-22).
passages.hearers:
‘Receive him as you would receive me.’ If Paul himself walked through the door, Philemon would welcome him with joy. Paul asks for the same welcome for Onesimus.

Then Paul steps between the two men. If Onesimus owes anything, ‘charge it to my account’. And he takes the pen himself: ‘I, Paul, write this with my own hand. I will repay it.’ It was like signing an IOU. Paul is not only asking Philemon to be generous. He is paying what it costs.

Then, gently, he adds that Philemon owes him ‘your very self’. Many take this to mean that Philemon came to faith through Paul. Whatever Onesimus owes Philemon, Philemon owes Paul far more.

In verse 20 Paul makes one more play on the name. ‘Let me have some benefit from you’ uses a word from the same root as Onesimus. Paul is saying, in effect, ‘Be an Onesimus to me.’ And ‘refresh my heart’ calls back to verse 7.

Paul is sure Philemon will do ‘even more than I ask’. He does not say what ‘more’ means. And then, ‘prepare a guest room for me’. Paul hopes to be released and to visit. He intends to see for himself how Onesimus was received.

Readers from Martin Luther onward have seen in verse 18 a picture of Christ, who takes our debt on himself and asks the Father to receive us as he would receive him. Luther said, in effect, that we are all Christ's Onesimus. That is a comparison, not a hidden meaning, but it fits the gospel Paul preached.
passages.ot:
Israel's law knew the duty of paying back what was owed: the one who had wronged his neighbour “must make restitution in full, add a fifth of the value, and pay it to the owner” (Leviticus 6:5). Here Paul pays someone else's debt.

And the welcome of an outsider into God's family echoes Ruth's words to Naomi: “your people will be my people, and your God will be my God” (Ruth 1:16).
passages.hard:
What did Paul hope Philemon would do? ‘You will do even more than I ask’ (verse 21) does not say.

Readers have answered in three main ways, and these readings can overlap. Many read the letter as asking at least that Philemon welcome Onesimus back without punishment, as a brother in Christ, and treat him as one from now on. Many read verse 16 and ‘even more than I ask’ as Paul's tactful way of asking Philemon to set Onesimus free. And many read verse 13, ‘I would have liked to keep him with me’, as a hint that Paul hoped Philemon would send Onesimus back to help him in his work. These notes do not choose.

We are not told what Philemon did. Some readers take the fact that this letter was kept and copied in the churches as a sign that he did what Paul asked. Ignatius of Antioch, early in the second century, names a bishop of Ephesus called Onesimus, and some think he was the same man. That is possible, but it cannot be proved.

What is plain is that Paul did not leave the matter to chance. He wrote in front of the whole church, paid what was owed, and said he was coming to see.
passages.asks: Paul pays a debt that was not his and asks for a welcome that was not owed. Ask whose debt you could carry, or whose wrong you could forgive, for Christ's sake. Ask who you would welcome as you would welcome a dear friend, and who you would not. And ask what ‘even more than I ask’ might mean for you.

passages.happening:
“Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends you greetings, as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers” (verses 23-24).

“The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
Five friends send greetings, and each has a story. Epaphras had first brought the gospel to Colossae (Colossians 1:7), and now he shares Paul's prison. Mark is John Mark, who had once turned back on Paul's first missionary trip and caused a sharp split between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:37-39); now he is a fellow worker again. Aristarchus came from Thessalonica and sailed with Paul to Rome (Acts 27:2). Luke was the doctor whom early writers name as the author of the Gospel and Acts (Colossians 4:14). And Demas would later leave Paul, ‘in his love of this world’ (2 Timothy 4:10).

So even the list of names tells of forgiveness given and received, and of how faithfulness is never automatic. Mark, who had once let Paul down, was later called ‘useful to me in the ministry’ (2 Timothy 4:11). Onesimus is being given the same chance.

The last line is a blessing of grace. The Greek says ‘your’ in the plural: Paul blesses the whole church in Philemon's house. Everything Paul has asked of Philemon, he asks inside that grace.
passages.ot: The blessing of grace goes back to the priests' words over Israel: “May the LORD bless you and keep you; may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you” (Numbers 6:24-25).
passages.asks: The names at the end tell of failure and restoration. Ask whether there is a Mark in your life, someone who once let you down, whom you could welcome back. Ask whether you are walking with Christ steadily, or drifting as Demas later did. And receive the last words as spoken to you: the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.
